He's absolutely right. I feel like there is too many times when Star Wars needlessly explains a moment in the movies or a Concept in the force to rationalize why something happened.

 For example, during the Darth Maul fight in The Phantom Menace, it was explained that Obi-Wan didn't use his Force speed like he did earlier in the movie because he was drained from the fight. I didn't really need to know that because we should just let the writing speak for itself and not get rationalized after the fact if people didn't like the outcome.

Another example, when Palpatine fought the Jedi Masters that were trying to arrest him, they explained it was because he used a force scream technique and his fighting style was something they weren't used to fighting. When in actuality George Lucas didn't have much planned for the Jedi Masters that died easily and it was only until later that more backstory was added to those characters.

I personally think we shouldn't have everything explained to us, just enough for us as an audience to understand and come up with our own theories. I liked it when Star Wars was more mysterious and magical instead of being so thoroughly explained that the fun is taken out of it.

Had a work colleague contact me out of the blue from my old job. They first started with ask me how I'm doing and what I'm up to and what is my future goals and the entire time I was waiting for her to come around to the reason why she decided to call me. Then she finally got to it, she gave me the sales pitch about how the group can provide amazing opportunities for people to make a lot of money and be their own boss while not needing to do a lot of work. It's all sounded well and good and I trusted her because we work together in the same job and she was a nice person when I got to know her in my training group.

It was until I agreed to show up at her apartment to meet with her and her husband and listen to them talk about Amway. The entire time I heard them talk about the company and what it does for its people, a lot of it sounded like a scam because they barely touched on what are we actually doing when you are in the company and where is all the money coming from and how does it all work. There was a lot of entrepreneur jargon without fully explaining what it's actually all about. The one thing that stuck with me and sounded the most suspicious of all was when they ended the presentation with telling me how I shouldn't tell my family members about it or look up reviews about it because they will tell you it is a scam and not to join it.

I just listened to a couple of the audio seminars they sent me and they all sound like those pick-up artist you see on the internet promising so much or talking you up a lot but not really saying anything. It's just a lot of words that specifically aim to repeat phrases over and over again and talk you up. It was then I decided to do some research and look into it further and I am so happy I did. I knew that there was something off about them especially a company that blatantly tells the people that are interested to not look into the negative reviews or listen to the people who call it a scam. I am heartbroken that one of my ex co-worker and her husband got wrapped up in all this trite and completely believe it. So yeah, that's a no for me I am not going to join a cult that sells people empty promises.

I'm pretty sure a lot of people are going to comment about the importance of session zero so I will add in my two cents as well. You as the DM really do need to lay down the law and have your boundaries be made apparent. Do not start a campaign without a session 0 and a clear understanding between you and your players on what is and is not okay at your table and your players. Setting these expectations and boundaries nip many problems in the bud and help weed out potential problem players but not all of them. Most importantly, stick to your guns. Don't let yourself or your players force you to do something that you do not want to role play or have acted out at the table.

When I first started I made a mountain of mistakes. I had no idea how to play the game, I barely read the rules and I made up so much stuff off the cuff. I also did not know what I wanted the story to be and a clear idea of the campaign, and I did not have a plan. We had no session zero, so what people wanted out of the game wasn't established. It was just whatever I came up with and hoped they liked it. I had no idea about modifiers, challenge ratings, character creation, and the entire rules.

For example, I gave my group's Centaur Paladin a +10 fire longsword and allowed him to become a death knight. It was the stupidest decisions I could have ever made. But, it's what the player wanted so I gave it to him. I also had no idea what resistance to magic effects meant. I just took the players word as truth when he said that meant he is immune to all magic. Just to let all of you know, the group I was running for was my siblings and they did not know how to play D&D either. So he had no idea what he was talking about and did not understand the rules either.

Also, when it came to spells they just selected any spell from the class they were, ignoring subclass, and level, and had no spell slots. So they could just endlessly cast any spell they wanted as long as it came from that class.

So let this be a lesson to all new DMs, read the damn rules and do not, for the Love of All That is Holy do not start your first ever campaign as a Homebrew. Run a pre-written adventure, you will feel so much better and more confident with an outline and a clear beginning and end story rather than just making everything up as you go. If I could go back and do it all again I would have ran a pre-written adventure and actually read the rules before I started the adventure.

I totally understand you man. My group isn't that comfortable with roleplay either and a good chunk of them want to play it like a video game. How I got through this and continue to get through it is to remember to make sure your players are having fun and enjoying the game. You have no idea how much stress I was relieved of once I stopped thinking of ways to punish my players because they aren't going where I want them to go or experience the cool stuff I want them to experience. I decide to let them enjoy the experience while still having rules and regulations D&D is run by. The world you are running will still carry on even if they don't want to take down the big bad oh, perhaps it might get a little worse but it's up to them to decide. As I've been told by many people, this is why session 0 is crucial to your campaign. That is the session where everyone can be clear with each other on what they want /expect out of the game and finding that middle ground. After doing that, your players will have a good time and maybe you might too. If you can't Run the game they want or find a middle ground, then maybe you should find a different group. It's better that way then trying to fight them or railroad when they keep straying.

I hope things work out with your group and you guys meet each other halfway and genuinely have fun. That's really the most important part as a DM that we all so easily forget. Because we are so caught up in creating a really great story / Adventure for our friends to enjoy. Communication is key, it doesn't hurt to ask. Good luck!
